title: Possession
full_review:
The romantic period-piece "Possession" (Focus) is a decided departure from director Neil LaBute's other disturbing films. However, this dreamy film with gorgeous countryside vistas and dripping romantic notions has some unpleasant elements, such as a mild lesbian relationship and an out-of-wedlock child, which may sour the otherwise fanciful story line for moviegoers. These aspects, while mostly peripheral, are included to heighten the sense of longing in a story about love, passion and mystery. Even so, their inclusion may be off-putting.

The film takes place in present-day England and follows a pair of literature scholars, cold Brit academic Maud (Gwyneth Paltrow) and cocky American researcher Roland (Aaron Eckhart, a LaBute regular), as they track the historical path of a famous (fictitious) Victorian-era poet, Randolph Henry Ash (Jeremy Northam), who had a secret extramarital affair with the love of his life, lesser-known poet Christabel LaMotte (Jennifer Ehle).

Floating back and forth between the present and the past, "Possession" is much closer to a Merchant-Ivory production, with its majestic imagery and gushy love story, than LaBute's previous films, such as the sordid "Your Friends and Neighbors" and the disturbing "In the Company of Men." LaBute co-wrote the adapted screenplay from A.S. Byatt's 1990 novel of the same title, which won the Booker Prize for Fiction. The script admirably condenses the comprehensive novel, layering in intrigue and obstacles to love. But it isn't able to avoid narrative lags, eventually resulting in a reasonably entertaining but not completely absorbing or dramatically compelling film.

As Maud and Roland further investigate the previously unknown relationship between the two poets, their only link with the past is a cache of love letters that appear to be from Ash to LaMotte. Ash is known to have been a legendarily faithful husband, while LaMotte was living with her lesbian companion, Blanche (Lena Headey). The discovery that the two had an affair would be the literary find of the century, which is partly what spurs Maud and Roland on.

As the two scholars read the gushing love letters aloud to each other and retrace the couple's secret love journey, romance and passion creep into their modern hearts and they are off in an obvious direction. But their courtship is filled with the usual hang-ups and complications of modern-day romances (namely fear of commitment) while Ash's and LaMotte's forbidden passion is colored by the rosy notion that true love is a risk worth taking. Yet it is Ash's and LaMotte's willingness to gamble all for their love that provides Maud and Roland with the encouragement they need to proceed.

Paltrow, with her flaxen hair tightly pulled back in a bun and once again assuming a mild British accent, offers a standard beautiful-woman-afraid-to-be-hurt-by-love performance. She is attractive and appealing, but nothing more. Eckhart is a little too intense in his portrayal, although the character is pretty one-dimensional. Both Northam and Ehle throw themselves into the roles, resulting in pleasing, but not outstanding performances.

"Possession" is mostly a sweetly enchanting story that washes over the viewer. Humorous touches cut the romance that oozes out of most scenes, keeping the sugary love affair between both couples in check. The film harks back to the days when the written word could stir more passion than the fieriest kiss.

Due to an extramarital affair, a sexual encounter, a lesbian relationship, a suicide and fleeting crass language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned that some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

(
2002
)
